content.title: Official Blind Review #1
content.review:
Short summary:
This paper builds a two-level hierarchical text classification model; with token classification at the bottom and sentences classification on top of token classification results. This work is closely related to a previous art (https://arxiv.org/pdf/1811.05949.pdf).  The model setup shares ideas with multi-task learning, in which the two separate tasks could be co-trained.

Novelties:
It extends the previous work by:
1) using separate head for each distinct tag label so that there is an explicit correspondence between attention heads and token labels.
2) due to 1), the classification extends to multi-labels naturally (instead of binary labels). 
3) a unique regularization term is introduced to enforce distinct representation sub-space for each of the query vector (head-specific). This is formulated in Eqn (13). 

Weakness:
* The novelties introduced above seem minor in my opinion. The importance of using the same number of heads for each distinct label is not tested or studied with ablation. In other words, with the normal setting of multi-head attention (with the head size not correlate with the size of tag label, for example, using fixed number of heads - 4 heads or 8 heads) thus not collapsing the queries into head-specific, would you get similar results? Is it really helpful to obtain a per-head representation to improve model performance on sentence-level classification? I know it probably helps human interpretation when you have per head representation. But beyond that, do you really get quality benefit?

* The experiment results would be more strong, if there are more reference base lines from the recent work. Currently all the models are different variations from this paper, except one trivial "random" model (Table 1 and Table 2).

* Another novelty ( bullet 3 above) introduced is the regularization term in Eqn 13. However, this does not have its own experiment. The current experiment (that involves this term) is always combined with two other changes (i.e. MHAL-joint). I will be interested to see experiment results (probably with another model with MHAL-sent + Rq or MHAL-sent+tok + Rq) to see if this additional regularization really helps.

* limitations of this model: 
  - since the number of heads is bound to be equal to the number of tags, the model would be difficult to scale when the tag vocabulary is large. In all the experimental dataset the author has worked with, the tag vocabulary size are all pretty small (from 3 to 6). 
  - It seems we always need a way to  map between token labels and sentence labels. This does not seem practical in a lot of text classification scenarios.
  - To get the max benefit from this model, we need good quality of token-level labels and sentence-level labels, which also seems not very practical in real NLP tasks.

content.title: Reply
content.comment:
Thank you for your valuable feedback and comments. We would like to address each concern in the same order.

* The main idea of the paper is to link two levels of text granularity: words and sentences. The hypothesis is that words compose together in a complex way to form sentences, and each hierarchical level encompasses some information about the other. A sentence of a certain kind (i.e. with a certain label) should have this reflected at the word level. To satisfy this hypothesis, the number of heads has to match the size of the tagset so that we can further combine these representations hierarchically. Your suggestion is interesting and worth trying, but under its framing, we would lose not only interpretability but also the main idea that this paper relies upon.

* Indeed, all of our baselines are different variations of the model proposed in this paper (MHAL). We did not find a model similar enough to fit the experimental settings and the tasks proposed. In this paper, we tried to emphasize the advantage one would get when exploiting the flexibility of DNNs to get intertwined representations, at two hierarchical levels that learn from each other. Our model is novel precisely in this respect.  Existing multi-task models do not address the same problem and are quite different ideologically. How we could use them to obtain results that would be meaningful and truly comparable to our model was not immediately obvious to us.

* We have performed such an ablation study, analyzing the contribution of each auxiliary loss when added on top of the baseline models (MHAL-sent and MHAL-sent+tok). We found that including the regularization term always helps. In particular, it gives the greatest performance boost when used in combination with the attention loss. Thank you for your suggestion, the next version of our paper will include this more detailed ablation study.

Regarding the limitations raised:

- We did not find that the model had difficulties scaling to a larger tagset, and this is due to the flexible multi-head architecture. However, our experiments show that, for tagsets of sizes greater than 8, the model does not learn attention evidence scores equally well across the heads because the labels are usually too sparse and noisy. Including other tasks or obtaining more examples (for the infrequent tags, in particular) are possible directions that could mitigate these effects and address this issue.

- The main idea of the paper is about exploiting an architecture that smoothly creates a map between tokens and sentences. We believe that this is a natural and desired property to have, motivated by how humans use language. Moreover, in this paper, we show that by jointly training the two tasks we always achieve better text classification performance.

- Indeed, we may need quality labels for the tokens and sentences, but the beauty of our model is that it does not require the expensive token-level tags for a whole big dataset to produce reasonable (fine-grained) tags for individual words. We argue that such a problem could be mitigated with MHAL. For instance, using our unsupervised model, we train a sequence labeler using only the sentence supervision signal. The labeling performance can be improved if the system is provided with a minimal amount (about 20-30%) of supervision on the words (this is our semi-supervised model, as described in the paper). The advantage offered by these two models is clear: they learn to perform sophisticated classifications, marking each word with a fine-grained label solely based on the sentence annotations (and these are considerably less expensive to obtain).

content.title: Official Blind Review #2
content.review_assessment:_thoroughness_in_paper: I read the paper at least twice and used my best judgement in assessing the paper.
content.review:
This paper studies the effects of joint learning of multi-level tasks: sentence classification and sequence labeling using a hybrid architecture of bidirectional LSTM and multi-head attention. They introduce a modification of the multi-head architecture to create a sentence representation and auxiliary objectives to enforce some relationship between the two tasks. The experiments comparing different settings of the models demonstrate that the models jointly learned using the two tasks are somewhat better than individual task-specific models. In addition, the zero-shot model also performs better than the baseline in the sequence labeling task.

This paper requires some clarification and more experiment results. I am leaning toward rejecting this paper for the following reasons:

It is unclear on the novelty of this paper’s contribution. It has been shown that multi-task learning objective is helpful. While the majority of recent work has focused on transfer learning (from LM objective) and weakly related tasks, the direction of the multi-level learning task has been explored to some extent, such as Hashimoto et al., 2017 (building from bottom-up) and Williams et al., 2017 (weakly supervised lower-level task). I think there should be more effort into distinguishing their findings from the previous. Additionally, the paper should build on top of a well-known architecture for a greater impact. For example,  using the multi-head attention architecture to perform classification is discussed in Devlin et al. 2018. A comparison with existing models, both theoretically and empirically, will be very helpful to readers.

The proposed method does not seem well justified by the experiment results. As mentioned previously, the paper lacks a comparison with existing models to justified architectural and training choices. Furthermore, the internal comparisons show that the proposed model has a small improvement from the individual models on both sentence-level and token-level tasks. As for the other auxiliary losses, we see all of their effects combined, rather than individual ones. The ablation analysis would be helpful. Finally, I think the zero-shot experiment is interesting. Unfortunately, we cannot draw a solid conclusion here. The MHAL-zero has an additional signal from the weak supervision from the proposed attention loss which is somewhat related to how the sentence labels are created (a big improvement on CoNLL-2003 and FCE). 

Clarification Questions:
1. How does this model work in the case of H != S and S > 2?
2. How is the LM loss computed? I.e. Which representations are used to predict word distribution?
3. In the semi-supervision experiment, I am not sure how you get “38% on SST, …” for MHAL-zero. Additionally, can you explain “Using only 30% of data, MHAL already approaches its fully-supervised performance”?

Hashimoto, Kazuma, et al. "A joint many-task model: Growing a neural network for multiple NLP tasks." arXiv preprint arXiv:1611.01587 (2016).

Williams, Adina, Andrew Drozdov, and Samuel R. Bowman. "Learning to parse from a semantic objective: It works. Is it syntax?" arXiv preprint arXiv:1709.01121 4 (2017).

Devlin, Jacob, et al. "Bert: Pre-training of deep bidirectional transformers for language understanding." arXiv preprint arXiv:1810.04805 (2018).

content.title: Reply
content.comment:
Thank you for your valuable feedback and comments. We address each of your questions below:

1. How does this model work in the case of H != S and S > 2?

In the case of H != S and S > 2, we concatenate the score obtained for the default head o_d with the linear projection of the scores obtained for the non-default heads o_nd onto a space of the size of the non-default sentence labels. Following the notation from the paper, we have o~ = [o_d; o_nd], where o_nd = W * concat_(for all h!=d)[o_h] + b. In practice, we did not find any datasets that satisfy this criterion i.e. datasets that have non-binary sentence labels and different cardinalities for the token and sentence label-sets. Since we could not test it, we decided not to mention it in the paper. It might be that such a setting is artificial and does not (ever or frequently) occur in reality. If you happen to know of a suitable dataset or task that fits this scenario, please let us know as we would be very interested in testing our model on it.

2. How is the LM loss computed? i.e. Which representations are used to predict word distribution?

The LM loss is computed as described in the paper by Marek Rei (2017) "Semi-supervised Multitask Learning for Sequence Labeling". We do not use the continuous representations obtained directly from the Bi-LSTMs since they contain information from both directions and thus they already have sufficient knowledge to make the LM task trivial. Instead, we use the hidden states outputted at every time step i by each of the two recurrent networks. We extract specialized features for language by passing these through a non-linear layer. Then, we map them to a probability distribution over the vocabulary using a softmax activation function. Please check the original paper for the extensive description and mathematical formulations.

3. In the semi-supervision experiment, I am not sure how you get "38% on SST, ..." for MHAL-zero. Additionally, can you explain "Using only 30% of data, MHAL already approaches its fully-supervised performance"?

Our precise phrasing was "We observe that adding as little as 10% of the token-annotated sentences increases MHAL-zero's performance by substantial amounts (38.01% on SST, ...)". By 38% we meant the difference between MHAL-zero's sequence labeling performance (on SST, this is 26.93%, as given in Table 2) and the performance of MHAL with 10% token-annotated sentences (on SST, this is 64.94%). We call this MHAL-10% as it is just MHAL allowed to learn about tokens using direct token supervision from 10% of the sentences, as described in our semi-supervised experiments. We did not explicitly provide the exact numbers in a separate table for the semi-supervised experiments as we thought that the numbers can be deduced from Figure 3.

"Using only 30% of data, MHAL already approaches its fully-supervised performance". Here, we wanted to compare the performance of MHAL-30% (trained under our semi-supervised setting) with MHAL-joint (trained under our fully supervised setting). More explicitly, we claim that by training our model using only 30% of the sentence-annotated tokens in the dataset, MHAL-semi-sup approaches its performance when trained as a fully supervised text classifier i.e. close to MHAL-100% = MHAL-joint = the right-most point in each plot in Figure 3.

content.title: Official Blind Review #3
content.review_assessment:_checking_correctness_: I assessed the sensibility of the derivations and theory.
content.review:
This paper addresses the problem of text classification by incorporating classification at both token and sentence levels, with the aim of better learning composition. The paper finds that introducing losses at multiple levels, along with additional auxiliary objectives, generally improves performance over simpler baselines.

The paper is clearly written, and I like the combination of token-level and sentence-level objectives with the aim of better learning compositional properties of language. I think the architecture described is interesting, with reasonable motivation, so overall I think the paper has potential. However, I don't think the paper in its current form has clear enough takeaways or strong enough results to make a publishable contribution -- in particular, it's not clear that the model in fact advances our ability to capture composition, nor do the results clearly advance the state of the art, and the contextualization with respect to related work is too minimal. 
 
The main claim of the paper is that this multi-level labeling scheme incentivizes the network to learn better composition functions. However, there is no compelling reason to conclude that composition has necessarily been improved here. The majority of tasks being tested on are not related to composition -- it seems that the token/sentence relationship in the error detection and entity detection tasks simply involves identifying whether one token in the sentence has a positive label, which really has nothing to do with composition. The SST task can plausibly require non-trivial composition to relate between the token-level sentiment and the sentence-level sentiment, but that would typically involve incorporating sentiment at the phrase level along the way, rather than jumping from the token to the sentence level, which seems more likely to focus on individual lexical cues rather than composition. Beyond the choice of tasks, there is also no further analysis/discussion to help in determining whether anything about composition has been improved. 

If the results were strong enough to advance the state of the art in these tasks, the composition takeaways might be less critical, but since the only baselines compared against are simpler versions of this model, it's not clear that the results here advance the state of the art in any way.

As another point: the contextualization with respect to related literature should also be improved. Currently the related work is described extremely briefly and fairly obliquely, and it is not clear how exactly this work differs from other work that has involved prediction at multiple linguistic levels (or work on composition).

Overall, I think the paper has potential, but it needs a clearer contribution and better contextualization.

content.title: Reply
content.comment:
Thank you for your valuable feedback and comments. The contribution we made is indeed subtle, but we think it is valuable and important. The question we ask is: can we explore the flexibility of a typical deep neural network architecture to create an implicit link between tokens and sentences? To test this link/mapping, we proposed the task of text classification because it makes it easy to attest to compositionality. Sentiment analysis is the most obvious example, but the rest of our tasks also reflect the aspect of compositionality. Take, for instance, error detection: there are 7 different labels for the tokens and only two for the sentences. Learning to label the sentences based on the token heads is easy, but the other way around is difficult. Moreover, the various errors span multiple words in a rather complex way (e.g. they are not necessarily neighboring words that together give rise to a certain grammatical error). There is an intricate aspect of compositionality in this task that we found worth exploring. We are open to suggestions, so please let us know of any tasks and datasets that reflect the compositional aspect of language and that can be applied to our idea of linking words and sentences.

Thank you for the suggestion of providing more contextualization. We found this to be a recurring issue in the reviews received, indicating that it requires more attention. We will include an extended related-work section in our updated version of the paper. We want to emphasize that the research topic proposed is (to the best of our knowledge) different from everything that has been published so far. The most similar, previous work has already been cited and briefly described (see Rei and Søgaard (2019), for instance). There is no other work exploring the relationship between the proposed levels of granularity. To re-iterate in plain terms the main finding of our paper: we take a DNN architecture for sentence classification, we allow the network to develop as a sequence labeler too (through each of the heads), and show that this natural change leads to better performances on both tasks, on each of the datasets tried. Linking the words to their sentences in this way is truly novel. That is why we did not find a system whose performance will be comparable to ours. We do not achieve state-of-the-art performance in any of the tasks proposed, but SOTA was not our explicit goal. We were more motivated by the idea and by its empirical proof.
